Plot1.funFact: Veld grape and dragon fruit  look very similar, often causing confusion among gardeners.

openarea2A.uses: Sericulture (Silk Production): White mulberry leaves serve as the primary, indispensable food source for silkworms.Culinary Arts: The sweet, tart fruits are eaten fresh or processed into jams, juices, wines, pies, and tarts.Traditional Medicine: Practitioners of Traditional Chinese Medicine use the root bark, leaves, and fruit to address coughs, fever, and blood sugar regulation.
openarea2A.funFact: Not a True Berry: Botanically speaking, a mulberry is not a berry at all but a "multiple fruit" formed from a cluster of independent flowers.Super-Sonic Pollen: The flowers of the white mulberry tree can fire pollen at over half the speed of sound, making it one of the fastest movements in the plant kingdom.

openarea2B.uses: Medicinal Infusions: In the Philippines, the leaves are widely boiled to create a medicinal tea used to treat coughs, diarrhea, colic, and dysentery
openarea2B.funFact: Namesake Origins: It gets its name from the Fujian Province in southeastern China (often spelled Fukien in the past), where it has been grown for centuries and is mentioned in literature dating back to the Tang Dynasty.

openarea2C.uses: Edible Greens: Highly nutritious and packed with protein and vitamins. The tender leaves are frequently boiled, stir-fried, or used as a nutrient-dense spinach substitute in soups, quiches, and omelettes. The flowers can be eaten raw in salads.
openarea2C.funFact: Explosive Seed Pods: The plant produces seed pods that, when ripe and dry, split in half explosively to fling their seeds out into the surrounding area.It’s Not Actually Chinese: Despite its common name, the Chinese Violet is native to sub-Saharan Africa and India

openarea2D.uses: Folk Medicine: Traditionally crushed, boiled, or dried to create herbal teas and poultices. It is empirically used to lower blood pressure, reduce cholesterol, manage diabetes, and heal wounds
openarea2D.funFact: It’s Not Actually an Onion: Despite resembling shallots with its red skin and white rings, the Dayak onion belongs to the iris family (the same family as saffron) rather than the allium family.Evening Bloomers: The plant produces small, delicate five-petaled white or yellow flowers that bloom in the late afternoon and stay open for only a few hours.

openarea2E.uses: Fresh Consumption: Eaten fresh out of hand when absolutely ripe (deep red or near-black) to avoid its bitter, resinous under-ripe tang.
openarea2E.funFact: Folk Remedies: Teas made from the leaves are used as a folk treatment for stomachaches, colic, bronchitis, and heartburn.Blood Pressure: Traditional extracts have been studied for their natural antihypertensive properties.

openarea2F.uses: The tree is primarily valued for its bright red-orange seeds, which provide a versatile natural pigment called annatto.Natural Food Coloring: It is one of the world's most common natural dyes, used to give cheese (like Cheddar), butter, margarine, ice cream, and rice their yellow or orange hues.
openarea2F.funFact: The Name Origin: The "lipstick tree" nickname comes from indigenous people in Central and South America using the seed pulp as a natural cosmetic and body paint for ceremonies.Ancient Sunscreen: The Mayans and Aztecs used the pigment not just for color, but as a natural sunscreen and insect repellent.

openarea2G.uses: Used in drinks, marinades, and desserts
openarea2G.funFact: Prevented scurvy in sailors; highly acidic fruit.

openarea2H.uses: Traditional Medicine: In Southeast Asia (especially Malaysia and Singapore), the raw or boiled leaves are used in folk medicine to treat cancer, rheumatism, gastric pain, and ulcers.Edible Fruits & Leaves: The fleshy, top-shaped yellow fruits are edible (though quite sour) and can be used in chili pastes or cocktails. The leaves can also be eaten raw in small quantities or used to make tea
openarea2H.funFact: A Cactus with Leaves: Unlike nearly all other cacti, the Rose Cactus does not drop its leaves; it retains large, glossy green leaves year-round.Ancient Ancestry: Because it retains true leaves, it is considered a "primitive" or non-succulent cactus. It is basically an evolutionary stepping stone between normal leafy shrubs and desert cacti!

openarea2I.uses: Culinary: The leaves are a staple leafy vegetable in many West and Central African cuisines (most famously in the Nigerian dish Ofe Onugbu). Because of their pungency, they are repeatedly squeezed and washed to remove excess bitterness before being added to stews.Traditional Medicine: The juice and leaf extracts are consumed as tonics or teas to alleviate malaria, control blood sugar in diabetics, and boost digestion.
openarea2I.funFact: Domestic Applications: The strong, bitter woody stems are frequently broken down and used as natural "chewing sticks" to maintain dental hygiene and ward off mouth infections.

openarea2J.uses: Skin Healing: It is widely known as the "ringworm bush". Crushed fresh leaves or sap contain chrysophanic acid, which naturally fights fungal infections like ringworm, athlete's foot, and eczema when applied topically.
openarea2J.funFact: The candle bush gets its name because its unopened bright-yellow flower spikes resemble giant, glowing, waxy candles!

openarea2L.uses: Insect Repellent: The oil contains natural compounds (like citronellal, geraniol, and limonene) that mask human odors, effectively deterring mosquitoes and other biting bugs [1].Aromatherapy: Used in diffusers to create a calming, refreshing atmosphere and to help relieve mental fatigue.Skincare & Cosmetics: Diluted into soaps, lotions, and massage oils [2]. It has natural antifungal and antibacterial properties that help cleanse the skin.
openarea2L.funFact: Not a single plant: People often assume citronella is a specific plant, but it is actually a tall, clumping grass similar to lemongrass

openareaM.uses: Culinary: The mushroom-flavored flowers are a popular, quirky addition to fresh salads. The tough flower spikes can also be used as a seasoning in soups and stews much like a bay leaf.Traditional Medicine: Historically used by indigenous and folk healers as a "cooling tonic". Leaves are frequently steeped into teas or decoctions to help soothe gastrointestinal discomfort, clear respiratory issues, and promote relaxation
openareaM.funFact: It tastes like mushrooms: The tiny, delicate flowers can be eaten raw and have a surprisingly distinct, earthy, mushroom-like flavor.It has a beer connection: The common name "porterweed" comes from the dark, foamy, beer-like infusion that can be made from brewing its leaves.

openarea2Q.uses: When ripe, they are dark red or purple, crunchy, and refreshing, similar to an apple. Used in soups, stews, porridges, and as a filling for Chinese desserts like mooncakes and mochi.
openarea2Q.funFact: Jujube fruit , also known as red dates  is a highly nutritious, versatile fruit cultivated for over 4,000 years, primarily in Asia

openarea2R.uses: Traditionally, various parts of the plant are used in Ayurvedic and other traditional systems of medicine to treat skin complaints, diarrhea, vertigo, fever, and body aches.  The ripe, dark purple or black berries are edible and have a tart, pleasant taste. They are sometimes used in jams and jellies.
openarea2R.funFact: The fruit is a favorite snack of the bandicoot, a small marsupial, which gives the plant its common name, Bandicoot Berry.

openarea2S.uses: This plant is a powerhouse in traditional medicine and regional cuisines across South and Southeast Asia:Medicinal Tea: The leaves are frequently brewed into a health-promoting tea, particularly in Thailand, to manage conditions like diabetes and rheumatism.
openarea2S.funFact: VapoRub Scent: When its leaves are crushed, they release a powerful, medicinal odor similar to camphor or Vicks VapoRub, which gives the plant its name.Antioxidant Powerhouse: Research suggests that tea made from Pluchea indica leaves can have stronger antioxidant properties than even green tea (Camellia sinensis). Coastal Guardian: This plant thrives in harsh, salty environments like mangroves and salt marshes, playing a vital role in maintaining the ecological balance of coastal areas.Natural Insect Repellent: Because of its pungent chemical glands, the plant is naturally resistant to deer and is often used as a biological insect repellent.

openarea2T.uses: Broom Production: Its long, feathery flower panicles are harvested and dried to create durable "light dust" brooms (often called phool jhadu) that are staples in households across South and Southeast Asia.
openarea2T.funFact: Disney Famous: This grass is planted extensively at Disneyland, particularly around the Jungle Cruise ride, to create an authentic tropical jungle atmosphere.

openarea2U.uses: Culinary & Snacks: Eaten roasted or salted, and blended into pastes as the creamy base for Indian curries (like Korma)
openarea2U.funFact: They Are Not True Nuts: Botanically, the cashew is actually a drupe (a seed that grows on the outside of a false fruit), rather than a traditional nut.A Poison Ivy Relative: The cashew tree is in the Anacardiaceae family, meaning it shares a botanical lineage with pistachios, mangoes, and toxic plants like poison ivy and poison oak

openarea2V.uses: Fresh Eating: Sliced raw and eaten fresh, often used as a garnish in salads, fruit platters, and cocktails.
openarea2V.funFact: Dietary Precaution: People with kidney problems or chronic kidney disease should avoid star fruit National Kidney Foundation. The fruit contains a neurotoxin (carambotoxin) and high levels of oxalates that healthy kidneys easily filter out, but can be dangerous or cause severe hiccups, vomiting, and confusion in individuals with kidney dysfunction.

The fruit contains a neurotoxin (carambotoxin) and high levels of oxalates that healthy kidneys easily filter out, but can be dangerous or cause severe hiccups, vomiting, and confusion in individuals with kidney dysfunction.

openarea2Y.uses: Culinary Snack (Emping): The mature seeds are ground into flour and deep-fried to create emping, a popular, slightly bitter Indonesian cracker.
openarea2Y.funFact: An Imposter "Fruit": Melinjo does not produce true fruits or flowers. It is a gymnosperm (related to pine trees), meaning its "fruits" are actually colorful, fleshy seed cones.

openarea2Z.uses: Culinary: Highly sour, it is used as a natural souring agent (like tamarind) in Asian curries, fish stews, and sambals. In Southeast Asia and the Philippines, the raw fruit is often dipped in rock salt or made into sweet jams and pickles.Traditional Medicine: The leaves, fruit, and flowers are used in folk medicine to treat coughs, high blood pressure, and skin conditions (like itchy rashes or mumps).
openarea2Z.funFact: Grows from the trunk: Unlike most fruits that hang from branches, belimbing fruits grow in heavy, clustered groups directly on the tree trunk and main branches.High productivity: A single tree can produce an astonishing 45 to 50 kg of fruit in a year.

openarea2ZZ.uses: Beverage production: Roasted and ground seeds are brewed into global beverage variants.Caffeine extraction: Isolates are utilized in pharmaceuticals, energy drinks, and supplements.
openarea2ZZ.funFact: Fruit origins: Coffee beans are actually seeds found inside bright red fruits called "coffee cherries".Goat discovery: Legend says 9th-century Ethiopian herders discovered coffee after seeing goats "dance" from eating the berries.
